subject: Post-demo: SDK auth & streaming behavior — request/response schema decisions
messages:
From: Maya Srinivasan <maya@redwood.com>
To: Tom Alvarez <tom@acmeanalytics.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, ben_carter@redwood.com
Date: Sun, 18 Jul 2027 14:03:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: SDK auth & streaming behavior — request/response schema decisions

Thanks for the demo today — appreciate the walkthrough, Tom. Quick recap and a few concrete items to decide so our engineering kickoff can be focused: 

1) Integration priorities (what we heard today)
   - SDK setup: Acme will embed Redwood client in a Java backend (Spring) + some lightweight Node services for webhooks.
   - Auth: you mentioned org-level API keys today; want to confirm whether you prefer scoped API keys, OAuth or mTLS for Prod.
   - Routing/fallback: regional preference (us-east) + cost-fallback to an equivalent lower-cost model.
   - Structured output / tool-calling: you want function-calling style JSON for 1) search queries and 2) external tool invocation.
   - Embeddings & reranker: two-tier pipeline: coarse embeddings for candidate retrieval (~1536-d), then a reranker model for final scoring.

2) Open request/response schema questions we need answers on:
   - Chat vs completions: which endpoints should hold session state? For the recommendation flow, do you want stateful chat (maintain conversation) or stateless completions per request?
   - Tokenization and max_tokens: how much headroom should we reserve in requests for system prompt + metadata + expected output?
   - Stop tokens: do you have application-level terminators we should encode?
   - Streaming semantics: do you want delta updates (partial JSON fragments) or a final-only response? If delta, how should partial JSON be encoded so we can reassemble cleanly?

Next steps I propose:
- You confirm preferred auth method (scoped API key vs OAuth vs mTLS) by Wed 7/21.
- We attach a small schema example (attached) and a minimal curl + SDK snippet; review and comment.
- Engineering access: provide a test dataset or credentials so Ben can validate tokenization/embedding sizes.

Attached: redwood-integration-skeleton.json (schema stub), acme-postcall-notes.pdf

Example quick guidance (high level):
- Recommend chat endpoint for flows that maintain short-lived state (recommendations with multi-turn clarifications). Use completions for single-shot templated outputs.
- Reserve 256-512 tokens for system/prompt overhead when you set max_tokens for responses for 2k context models.
- Prefer scoped API keys for self-service + rotation; use mTLS for private on-prem installs or if your security team requires certificate auth.

Thanks — I can host a short tech sync next week to lock these down.

—
Maya Srinivasan
Solutions Lead, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-demo: SDK auth & streaming behavior — request/response schema decisions

Tom — quick answers and a couple of concrete examples attached inline.

1) Streaming + partial structured responses

- Pattern we use: stream "delta" events as text/plain chunks that wrap a top-level envelope (event-type + fragment-index + chunk). On the client, you reconstruct fragments deterministically by index. Example chunk: {"event":"delta","idx":1,"payload":"{\"tool\":\"search\",...}"}
- For strict JSON outputs we recommend function-calling / structured responses where the runtime returns a final canonical JSON object at the end and intermediate deltas are encoded as base64 blocks (if you require exact parseability mid-stream). That avoids partial-JSON parse errors.

2) Tokenization & multilingual concerns

- Redwood token counting for costs uses the same tokenizer family as the model you pick (BPE/byte-level). For mixed-language inputs we recommend measuring token density on a 1k-sample using our token counter tool (we can run this if you share samples).
- Reserve ~30-40% overhead for system prompts + metadata for short-context models; for long-context (>=32k) reserve less (10-15%).

3) Reranker latency guidance

- For a basic rerank step on a single GPU: scoring 200 candidates with a mid-sized reranker typically appears in 40–120ms P90 with optimized batching; depends on model choice and quantization. We can provide a perf profile for the exact reranker you plan to use once you share the model id.

4) Chat vs completions decision matrix

- Use chat if you need persistent conversation state, message roles, or system-level instructions.
- Use completions for single prompt -> single response flows, especially when you control prompt composition entirely and want deterministic stop-token behavior.

Attached inline is a minimal curl + Node SDK example showing a streaming chat call with delta events. If helpful, Ben can follow up with a small test harness to exercise tokenization and chunking.

—
Maya

Adding a few practical engineering notes so we can scope the POC: 

- max_tokens math: server-side you should compute available tokens = model_context - (system_tokens + estimated_user_tokens + reserved_margin). For 8k models I typically reserve 200–400 tokens for margin depending on truncation policy.
- Stop tokens: use explicit stop arrays when you control generation. For function-calling JSON, prefer final validation (schema check) rather than relying solely on stop tokens — models occasionally emit extras.
- Embeddings chunking: when you chunk long docs for retrieval, target ~400–800 tokens per chunk for 1536-d embeddings to balance recall and index size. That maps to ~300–600 words depending on language.
- Batching & throughput: enable request batching on the worker side for embeddings and reranker calls; we can recommend batch sizes per GPU once you confirm model variant.

Also: can you create a test service account (scoped) for our infra so Ben can run a tokenizer sweep over your sample docs? We won't use Prod keys.

Attaching schema-example.json as a draft.

—Ben
Principal Engineer, Redwood Inference
